accuracy.evidence: Every pattern and example word was checked against English Appendix 1 of the national curriculum in England (Years 3–4): /k/ spelt ch, Greek (scheme, chorus, chemist, echo, character); /ʃ/ spelt ch, mostly French (chef, chalet, machine, brochure); /g/ spelt -gue and /k/ spelt -que, French (league, tongue, antique, unique); /s/ spelt sc, Latin (science, scene, discipline, fascinate, crescent). Extra words were checked in the Online Etymology Dictionary: anchor was dropped from the sorter because its ch is an unetymological 16th-century spelling, not Greek, and replaced with stomach (Greek stomakhos); chute and parachute are French; chemist reached English through French and Medieval Latin from Greek, and is kept because the national curriculum lists it under Greek ch. The sc rule is stated as the soft-c rule (c before e, i or y says /s/), so scarf, scab, scoop, scale and scold correctly say /sk/; muscle, where sc sits before l, was left out on purpose because it breaks the simple rule.

misconceptions.evidence: The documented Year 3–5 slips are each targeted: phonetic spelling of the /k/ and /sh/ sounds (kemist, korus, shef, masheen in the proofreading step and the gap builder's k, c and sh tiles), dropping the silent u and e (leeg, leage, uneek, the g and k tiles in the endings step), dropping the silent c (sience, sene), thinking sc always says /s/ (step 4 prediction and the scarf/scab/scoop words) and reading every ch as the chip sound (step 1 prediction on chorus). The adult text also warns about over-applying the patterns (baque for back).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagorigin is built around where a spelling comes from: a three-way ch sound sort labelled Greek, French and everyday English with the ch underlined in each word, a gap builder whose tiles are the English, Greek and French spellings of one sound plus a meaning line, an ending builder for -gue and -que, an sc sort driven by the letter after sc, and a proofreader that turns sound spellings into the right ones. Existing spelling labs (flagaltsp alternative spellings, flagexcept tricky words, flagsfxrule suffixes, flaghphone homophones) have none of these; lab_distinct passed under 30% against every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child discovers the rule from feedback before the text names it: dropping chorus on 'ch: chip' returns 'Say chorus aloud: ch says k, as in kit. Greek words spell /k/ with ch'; choosing g for league returns 'league ends with gue. The u and e are silent, but you still write them'; dropping scarf on 'sc says s' returns 'the letter after sc is a, o or u, so the c is hard: sc says sk'. Each step closes with a one-line rule only after all the words are placed.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions each hold the tempting wrong answer: 'ch, as in chip' for chorus (disproved by the sound sort), 'sh, like ship' for machine (disproved by the gap builder, which rejects sh with a French-spelling message) and 'yes, always' for sc saying s (disproved when scarf, scab, scale, scoop and scold land in the sk box). The completion line names the learner's own pick.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions with every wrong option tagged to its own slip: 'sh' (French spells /sh/ with ch), 'dbl' (no double letter), 'eng' (everyday English spelling where a French or Greek pattern applies), 'fr' (that ch says sh, so French not Greek), 'drop' (silent u and e left out), 'soft' (sc before e or i says s) and 'k' (chorus is Greek, so /k/ is ch). Proofreading feedback inside the lab is also per slip (kh, c for k, missing u, wrong vowels in science).

readability.evidence: Measured with learn/readability.py: kid FK grade 0.7 (family limit 5.0) and adult 8.5 (limit 10.0). Kid sentences are short and concrete ('Here sc says s. Look at the next letter.'); sounds are written as plain letters (k, sh, s) for the child, with IPA only in the adult text. Every gap word has a plain meaning line so the child knows which word to build.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph teaches one pattern with examples; the adult text gives the curriculum source, the unifying idea (history, not sound, settles the spelling; sc follows the soft-c rule), named mistakes and what the lab does. The content gate found no filler phrases and the explanation is under 12% the same as every other lesson.

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px Android screenshots in light and dark for all six steps: the three ch trays fit one row with one-line labels, the underlined ch/sc stays centred in the word card, gap tiles are 58 px tall in one row, the meaning line sits under the gap card, and the proofreading options are full-width 58 px buttons. The 'This is how it sounds' line overlapped the misspelling card in the first screenshot and was moved below it. The browser walkthrough passed on iPhone 13.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button under the canvas: tray names with the current word in each aria-label ('chorus: k: Greek'), 'Fill the gap with ch', and 'Spelling: chemist'. Tapping a tray also posts the word; tiles can be dragged or tapped. The canvas aria-label is rewritten after each action with the feedback text, challenge feedback is a role=status live region, and axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) found no violations in either theme on desktop and iPhone 13.

sources: Department for Education (2013) The national curriculum in England: English Appendix 1, Spelling, Years 3 and 4 (words with /k/ spelt ch, /ʃ/ spelt ch, -gue and -que endings, /s/ spelt sc)
Online Etymology Dictionary (etymonline.com) entries for anchor, chemist, chute and orchid, used to check the extra example words
